title: A Leaked CIA Red Cell Warns Israel Could Face Civil War or Collapse Weeks Before Its Election, as China Opens a Third Overseas Base in Laos and Deploys Anti-Ship Missiles Near Taiwan
subhead: US intelligence analysts warn that economic strain, the conscription crisis and political breakdown could fracture Israel from within ahead of the October 27 vote, while Beijing expands its military footprint across Southeast Asia and the Taiwan Strait.

sections.heading: Leaked CIA analysis warns Israel risks 'civil war' and state collapse
sections.body:
A classified CIA assessment, reportedly titled 'Split from Within', warns that Israel could be heading toward civil conflict or what the report calls 'total collapse', according to Drop Site News, which first published the findings, with Middle East Eye, Anadolu Agency and Press TV corroborating the account. The assessment was reportedly produced by a Red Cell — an internal CIA device meant to challenge the agency's own consensus — and identifies converging pressures: sustained economic strain, a widening conscription crisis between ultra-Orthodox and secular Israelis, violence by Israeli settlers, trauma among returning soldiers, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's effort to stay in power.

The timing is what makes it significant. Israel votes on October 27 in its first election after a full Knesset term since 1988, and Al Jazeera and The Guardian report a genuinely contested race between Netanyahu and former war cabinet member Gadi Eisenkot, with polls from different broadcasters diverging sharply. The leak reflects a US intelligence community worried less about Israel's external enemies than about its internal cohesion — a shift in how Washington appears to be modelling its closest Middle East ally.
sections.whyItMatters: If a US assessment is genuinely flagging civil-conflict risk in Israel, that changes how Washington plans for the post-election period and how it weighs any new regional escalation. Internal fracture in Israel would ripple through every US contingency plan in the Middle East.

sections.heading: China opens its third overseas base and hardens its Taiwan flank
sections.body:
The People's Liberation Army opened the China-Laos Military Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun, Laos, on September 29 — its third overseas facility after Djibouti and Cambodia, according to the Institute for the Study of War's China-Taiwan update. ISW notes it is the PLA's first overseas base oriented around air power, with a runway of up to 6,562 feet, sited about 40 miles north of Vientiane near the Thai border. China's Ministry of National Defense framed it as a training site for Lao pilots. ISW also ties the base to Laos's deep financial dependence on Beijing, including $10.5 billion of debt — roughly 82 percent of Laotian GDP as of 2024.

In parallel, the US Marine Corps is preparing to fire anti-ship weaponry during exercises on a remote Japanese island near Taiwan, Defense News reports — the US, in effect, hardening the first island chain. Beijing responded to recent Japan-Philippines security talks by launching a maritime operation in the South China Sea, per the Beijing Post, while Taiwan's military tracked 16 Chinese ships around the island. Japan's new Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described China as 'an important neighbor' amid the Taiwan tensions, per Anadolu, even as The Diplomat described Japanese anxiety about being sidelined by a Trump-Xi deal.
sections.whyItMatters: China is converting economic leverage into permanent military access in Southeast Asia while the US and Japan build a distributed anti-ship posture around Taiwan. The Laos base extends China's reach toward the Malacca Strait and disputed South China Sea waters that sit astride global shipping.

sections.heading: Yemeni forces retake the Bab el-Mandeb approaches as Turkey and Pakistan commit troops to Saudi Arabia
sections.body:
Yemen's internationally recognised government said its forces retook the Red Sea port city of Mocha and positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from the Houthis, according to Al Jazeera, Reuters, Xinhua, Arab News and Al-Monitor. The military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes in the operation, and NDTV reported forces had retaken the town of Dhubab just north of the strait. Control of the Bab el-Mandeb — the chokepoint between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden — had slipped toward the Houthis through September.

The retaking coincided with emergency talks in Riyadh, where Turkey and Pakistan agreed to send forces to Saudi Arabia under their Mecca Pact mutual-defence commitments, Al Jazeera and Firstpost report. The Houthis nonetheless claimed strikes on Riyadh's airport and other Saudi sites, per AFP, and AFP also reported the group had effectively encircled Taiz. Taken together, the Red Sea is shifting from an attritional Houthi campaign toward a multi-nation counter-offensive with Turkish and Pakistani boots on Saudi soil.
sections.whyItMatters: The Bab el-Mandeb carries a large share of Europe-Asia trade. A Turkish-Pakistani troop deployment to Saudi Arabia turns a Yemeni civil war into a test of a new Sunni security bloc and widens who has a stake in the Red Sea.

sections.heading: Ukraine fires one of its largest drone waves at Moscow as diplomacy stalls
sections.body:
Ukraine sent roughly 650 drones toward the Moscow region overnight, Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, according to TASS and Reuters. Sobyanin reported 18 UAVs destroyed near the capital in one update before the count climbed to at least 81, per News.ru, and Ukrainian outlets reported the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya was hit. Moscow-area airports were reported paralysed during the attack. It was among the largest single drone waves of the war aimed at the Russian capital.

The strike landed as the diplomatic track frayed. President Zelensky said the US proposed trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine by the end of October, per the Kyiv Independent, but Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected a frontline freeze as a basis for talks, the Kyiv Post reports. India, meanwhile, has stepped into the gap: PM Narendra Modi said Delhi is intensifying its peace efforts, and Kyiv called India's ceasefire proposal the 'broadest' of four on the table, per the Indian Express and ThePrint.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is demonstrating it can still reach deep into Russia even as US-brokered talks falter, which weakens Moscow's claim that its rear is secure and raises the cost of a frozen-frontline deal. India's emergence as a mediator gives Moscow a channel that is not Washington.

sections.heading: Trump calls the Iran war nearly over, but Hormuz stays shut and tankers keep getting hit
sections.body:
President Trump said the war with Iran is 'essentially almost over' and that Tehran has 'virtually given up' any nuclear ambitions, per Iran International, TASS and Anadolu. The remarks contrast with conditions on the ground: Iran's president called talks with Washington 'meaningless' via state media, Tehran said the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until seven conditions are met, per Gulf News and The Online Citizen, and further tankers were reported hit near the strait, according to Iran International and the World Ports Organization. The US Navy has redirected about 130 vessels amid Iran's naval blockade, Gulf News reports.

Markets read the signals as easing. WTI fell below $90, trading near $88.60 early on October 6, as Middle East crude exports rebounded and the G7's 100-million-barrel reserve release added supply, per FXStreet and FXBus. InvestingLive reported Hormuz crude flows recovering to near 76 percent of pre-war levels, though it noted diesel shortages persist. Al Jazeera has also raised the question of whether Iran is quietly charging a toll on transiting oil.
sections.whyItMatters: A gap is opening between political rhetoric in Washington and the physical state of the strait. Traders are pricing de-escalation while Iran keeps the chokepoint closed — a mismatch that can reverse quickly if a tanker attack escalates further.

sections.heading: Brussels lets defence money pay for winter energy as Europe braces for a supply crunch
sections.body:
The European Commission told member states they may temporarily redirect part of their defence spending toward winter energy security, the Brussels Post reports — an unusual blurring of military and energy budgets. The move comes as Europe tries to fill storage before winter while phasing in a ban on Russian LNG from January 2027; Modern Diplomacy describes a looming 'cliff' where the ban collides with low inventories. Germany and Ukraine also signed an €8.5 billion package of defence and energy agreements, including Diehl and Hensoldt air-defence systems and interceptor drones, per IEU Monitoring.

The fiscal strain is uneven. Modern Diplomacy notes that while richer European states can finance rearmament, the bloc's weakest budgets cannot, and Germany's Bild-reported strain is echoed by analysts warning that welfare and energy costs compete directly with defence. Al Jazeera reported earlier that Washington pressed Europe to release emergency diesel stocks, with US gas prices above $7 a gallon, and Adalytica flagged risks across oil, diesel and LNG.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is discovering that rearmament and winter energy security draw on the same shrinking fiscal space. Letting defence funds pay for fuel is a signal that the continent's dual war-economy and cost-of-living pressures are colliding.

bottomLine: Today's clearest signal came from Washington's own analysts: a leaked CIA Red Cell warns that Israel — a cornerstone US ally — could fracture from within ahead of its October 27 election, a risk that sits awkwardly alongside Trump's insistence that the Iran war is nearly won. At the same time China quietly opened a third overseas military base in Laos and pressed its maritime campaign near Taiwan, while Yemeni forces retook the Bab el-Mandeb approaches and Turkey and Pakistan agreed to send troops to Saudi Arabia. Oil slipped back below $90 on the G7 reserve release and recovering Gulf exports, but Iran kept Hormuz shut and more tankers were struck — leaving a market priced for calm against a strait still closed. Ukraine's 650-drone wave on Moscow and Lavrov's rejection of a frontline freeze showed the Russia track is not close to a deal either.
